prize_parts.citation: For introducing firm heterogeneity and selection into trade theory, and for showing how reallocation across firms shapes exporting and the gains from trade.

statement.case_for: My configuration has changed. In round 1 I preferred B050 (Kiyotaki and Moore). I now prefer B038, a two-name Melitz-Helpman prize, with B050 as my first alternative. The change comes from applying one standard to every candidate: how directly the evidence tests the specific mechanism being credited, not only whether the idea has been influential. The chair's cross-candidate question asks the committee to state such a standard. On B050 I conceded that the post-2008 evidence shows financial frictions matter but does not validate the collateral-amplification channel itself. I weight that gap more heavily now. For B038 the credited mechanism is selection into exporting and reallocation across heterogeneous firms. It generates predictions that can be checked against firm-level customs and production data, and two decades of use have given that evidence time to accumulate and be challenged. The attribution is also reasonably contained: Melitz (2003) is the core model, and Helpman's firm-level work, including exports versus FDI with Melitz and Yeaple, is its natural complement. I would word the citation around the mechanism and not around the size of the welfare gains. B050 remains a serious candidate. Its attribution is the cleanest on the shortlist and its conceptual contribution is foundational. I have moved because I weigh direct testability a little more than attribution tidiness when the two conflict, not because I think the Kiyotaki-Moore contribution is lesser. I do not use the four explicit B038 supporters in round 1 as evidence of merit.
statement.case_against: My reservations about B038 are as follows. Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum have serious claims on closely related firm-level trade work, and they are outside the credited names. A Melitz-Helpman prize could therefore look incomplete. Firm-level exporter facts, such as exporter premia, were documented before the model, so some of the apparent empirical fit is accommodation of known facts and not out-of-sample prediction. That is a metascience concern I take seriously. The gains-from-trade magnitudes are also sensitive to elasticity and functional-form assumptions. Finally, the 2008 trade prize creates a possible overlap, although I read firm selection as a distinct, later discovery. For B050, the main weakness is the direct empirical identification of the collateral channel, together with possible thematic overlap with the 2022 prize.

responses.point: Friberg argues that the firm-level exporter facts were documented before the Melitz model, which then explained them. The strongest confirmation is therefore the selection and reallocation mechanism, not the size of the welfare gains, and the citation should rest on the former.
responses.response: This is the point that most affects how I weigh B038, and I read it through a replication and prediction lens. A model that fits facts already known is weaker evidence than one whose novel predictions were confirmed afterwards. Whether the selection and reallocation predictions held up out of sample, for example in responses to trade liberalisation, is the question I would want the committee to answer. As I understand the literature, such tests exist and broadly support the qualitative mechanism, but I have not independently verified this. Your reading is why I would word the citation around selection and reallocation and not around gains-from-trade numbers. It also leaves me less certain than a simple count of B038 supporters would suggest.

responses.point: Strömberg ranks B050 first with Kiyotaki and Moore. He concedes that direct identification of the collateral-amplification channel is mixed, that much of the confirming evidence comes from the adjacent accelerator and intermediary literature, and that the 2022 prize may overlap in theme.
responses.response: I agree with all three of your caveats, and they are the reason I moved. Our shared two-name attribution still holds, and I still think B050 passes the attribution test more cleanly than any other candidate. Peter Fredriksson asked you whether it clears the bar he applies to B036, and on attribution I think it does. The difficulty is on the evidence side, where you and I both concede that post-crisis support is for financial frictions in general. If the committee applies a single standard of direct validation of the specific credited channel, B050 is weaker on it than B038. That is a difference in the evidence and not a difference in the originality of the contribution. I would not object strongly if the committee chose B050 on the strength of its attribution.

responses.point: Boppart accepts that a two-name Kiyotaki-Moore set is better defined than adding Gertler. He still ranks B038 slightly higher because the empirical identification of the original collateral-amplification mechanism is more mixed than its theoretical influence.
responses.response: I have moved to the ordering you describe, for the same reason: the empirical record for the specific mechanism. I also agree with your wording on B038, that the citation should describe the firm-selection model and its welfare implications and not the whole firm-level trade literature. That is the best answer I can see to the Bernard-Eaton-Jensen-Kortum concern. It narrows the claim to what the credited names did without implying that others' contributions are lesser. I do not think it fully removes the risk that the set looks incomplete, and I record that as open.

responses.point: Fredriksson prefers B036 (Autor, Hanson, Katz), arguing that quasi-experimental local-labour-market evidence combined with a conceptual framework has been replicated and challenged over more than a decade. He accepts that Dorn in place of Katz is defensible, and that the boundary of the discovery is unclear.
responses.response: The quasi-experimental identification in B036 is the kind of evidence I weight heavily, and that is why it stays among my alternatives. I did not make it my preferred part for the reasons you give yourself. It bundles two strands with different authorship, and I cannot say whether Katz or Dorn is the right third name. How much task-model credit belongs outside the credited set also affects it. In my opening I proposed Autor, Hanson and Katz, and your point that Dorn is a core co-author of the trade-shock papers weakens my confidence in that trio. The ongoing debate about the size and persistence of the China-shock estimates adds to my hesitation. If the committee defines the achievement as the broader account of technology, tasks and trade, I could support B036. On the current record B038 is better bounded.

responses.point: Hassler ranks B015 first with Woodford, Taylor and Calvo. He sees dated, identifiable building blocks, a framework revised but not displaced through 2008 and 2021-23, and he acknowledges that omitting Galí, Gertler, Christiano, Eichenbaum and Smets is a real cost.
responses.response: I do not question the maturity or the influence of B015. The chair's question is what evidence would count as confirming the credited building blocks as distinct from the framework. I do not think survival through 2008 and 2021-23 answers it. Friberg notes that micro evidence on time-dependent versus state-dependent price adjustment is mixed. Persistence of a workhorse framework shows it is useful and adaptable, which is different from showing that Calvo pricing or the Taylor contract and rule were confirmed as stated. With eight credited names and three places, the credit also cannot be assigned cleanly. I have therefore not moved B015 into my own configuration. I would reconsider if the committee settled one citation, either origins plus synthesis or the canonical estimated model, and showed which evidence tests that specific claim.

uncertainties: Whether the selection and reallocation predictions of the heterogeneous-firm model have been confirmed out of sample, or whether much of the empirical fit is accommodation of previously documented exporter facts. I have not independently verified this.
Whether a two-name Melitz-Helpman set will look incomplete given Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum, and whether a mechanism-focused citation is enough to answer that.
Whether the 2008 trade prize reduces the case for a second trade award. I read firm selection as a distinct discovery, but that is a committee judgement.
Whether the committee applies the same standard of direct validation to theory-led candidates (B050, B021, B015) as to microdata-based ones (B038, B036), and what that standard is.
How to define B036 as one discovery or two, and whether Katz or Dorn is the right third name.
I rely on general knowledge of the literature and the supplied round-1 statements, and I have not independently verified any of the scientific or credit claims.
statement.conflict_note: No tie to the preferred part is apparent from my supplied profile. Melitz, Helpman and Redding are not among my listed co-authors or institutional contacts, and neither are the credited names on B050 and B036. My listed co-authors (Camerer, Pfeiffer, Holzmeister, Huber, Nosek, Johannesson, the Harvard evolutionary-dynamics network and Brodeur) do not appear among the credited names for any shortlisted ballot. I disclose an SSE affiliation shared with committee members Friberg and Strömberg, as Andersson also noted, and a long co-authorship with Magnus Johannesson (SSE), a former committee member. Friberg and Strömberg are both addressed above, and I treat their arguments as evidence only. My metascience background may lead me to overweight direct empirical validation when comparing candidates. I have tried to apply the same criteria across fields and have not adjudicated these ties.
